svg.aria-label: Diagram: how CloudWatch alarm tag propagation works, where the tags travel, and why the two filter modes differ for tags that do not yet exist. AWS announced support for including alarm tags in action payloads and EventBridge events so customers can route and filter alarm notifications by tag without additional lookups. When enabled on an alarm, CloudWatch adds the alarm tags to the messages it sends to Amazon SNS, AWS Lambda and Amazon EventBridge each time the alarm changes state. The setting is off by default and configurable per alarm, supported for metric, composite and log alarms, and available in all Regions where CloudWatch is available except Middle East UAE and Middle East Bahrain. The destinations behave differently in one important respect: CloudWatch sends alarm state change events to EventBridge by default, so configured tags appear in those events even when no action is configured on the alarm, whereas for Amazon SNS and Lambda tags appear only when that action is configured. Enabling propagation is therefore not scoped by the actions configured, and anything already consuming CloudWatch alarm events, such as a shared rule or a third-party integration, begins receiving the tags without being changed. For Amazon SNS, CloudWatch includes the tags in the notification message delivered to the topic's subscribers, including those using the HTTP/HTTPS and email protocols, so tags become email and webhook content, which matters because cost centre, owner email address and ticket reference are common alarm tag values. Tags are not propagated for several other action types, specifically Systems Manager OpsItems, Systems Manager Incident Manager incidents, Amazon EC2 actions, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling and Application Auto Scaling actions, and CloudWatch investigations, and tag keys beginning with aws colon are reserved for AWS and are never propagated, so CloudFormation and Auto Scaling generated tags stay out without being listed. The central finding concerns the three filter modes and how they treat tags added in future. By default, when tag propagation is enabled, CloudWatch includes all of the alarm's tags, and future tags as well if they are added later. With Exclude tag keys, CloudWatch includes all of the alarm's tags except the keys specified, and any tags added later are also included unless their keys are in the exclude list. With Include tag keys, CloudWatch includes only the keys specified, and if a new tag is added later and is wanted in the payload its key must be added to the include list. So the two filter modes fail in opposite directions for tags that do not exist at configuration time: an exclude list is open by default, meaning a tag created next year is published unless somebody remembers to extend the list, while an include list is closed by default, meaning a new tag is withheld until somebody extends it. An exclude list can only name the keys that existed when it was written, which makes it the wrong instrument for keeping a class of value out of notifications, and the include list is the one that fails safe at the cost of maintenance when a new tag should travel. That is the right cost to pay, because forgetting to add a key loses a routing dimension while forgetting to extend an exclude list publishes something. Each notification or event reflects the alarm's tags at the time of the state change, including tag changes made after the alarm was created, so a retag takes effect on the next transition with no republish needed and a mistaken retag is live immediately. Every payload carries a status field, AlarmTagsStatus for Amazon SNS and alarmTagsStatus for Lambda and EventBridge, with four values. SUCCESS means the tags were retrieved and any key filter was applied, and the list can be empty if the filter excluded all tags, so SUCCESS does not imply tags are present. NO_TAGS means the alarm has no tags. TRUNCATED means some tags were omitted to keep the payload within its size limit, with the documented remedy being to narrow the set using the include or exclude options. FAILURE means the tags could not be retrieved when the notification was sent, and CloudWatch still delivers the notification or event with no tags, so the message arrives on time looking exactly like an alarm on an untagged resource, and the only thing distinguishing a missing owner tag from an unreadable one is the status field. A router that branches on the presence of a tag will therefore silently take the wrong branch, which means any consumer routing on tags must read the status field and define an explicit fallback. The representation differs by destination: SNS and Lambda include the tags as a list of key-value objects while EventBridge includes them as key-value pairs to make event pattern filtering easier, which shows the routing case was designed for rather than merely accommodated, since a list of objects is awkward to match in an event pattern and key-value pairs are not. A consequence is that an EventBridge rule can now match on a tag value, making an edit to an alarm's tags a routing change. On permissions, a principal that creates or updates an alarm to enable this configuration must have the cloudwatch ListTagsForResource permission for that alarm, which is coherent since enabling propagation asks CloudWatch to read tags on the customer's behalf indefinitely, and CloudWatch provides a dedicated cloudwatch AlarmTagsPropagationEnabled condition key to control whether principals can enable tag propagation at all, a separation that lets an organisation permit alarm creation while withholding the ability to turn propagation on. On the API, tag propagation is enabled by setting the AlarmTagsPropagation configuration within the ActionConfiguration parameter on PutMetricAlarm, PutCompositeAlarm or PutLogAlarm with Enabled set to true, DescribeAlarms returns the current configuration so the setting is auditable across an account without a new API, IncludedTagKeys and ExcludedTagKeys are mutually exclusive, omitting both includes all tags, and each list can contain from 1 to 50 tag keys with each key from 1 to 128 characters. The recommended actions are to list the distinct tag keys and values on the alarms in scope before enabling anything and decide which would be acceptable in an email, to choose an include list rather than an exclude list unless there is a specific reason, to use the condition key to decide centrally who may enable this, to make consumers read the status field and define the fallback for FAILURE and TRUNCATED explicitly rather than treating an absent tag as an untagged alarm, to check what already consumes alarm events in EventBridge since those get the tags regardless of configured actions, and to audit with DescribeAlarms once enabled.
svg.title: Include is closed for future tags; exclude is open for them
svg.text: An exclude list can only name the tags that existed when you wrote it.
CloudWatch alarm tags in action payloads — off by default, per alarm, three filter modes.
The two filter modes fail in opposite directions, and only on tags that do not exist yet
neither list today: published later: “future tags as well if they are added later”
ExcludedTagKeys today: unless listed later: PUBLISHED — “also included, unless their keys
are in the exclude list”
IncludedTagKeys today: only if listed later: WITHHELD — “you must add its key to the
include list”
Forget to extend an include list and you lose a routing dimension. Forget an exclude list and you publish something.
Further than the action you configured
EventBridge gets them “even when you don't
configure an action on the alarm”.
SNS delivers to subscribers “including those
that use the HTTP/HTTPS and email protocols”.
Cost centre. Owner email. Ticket ref. In an email.
Two of four statuses mean “cannot route”
SUCCESS may still be an empty list
NO_TAGS the alarm has none
TRUNCATED some omitted for size
FAILURE delivered anyway, with no tags
FAILURE looks exactly like an untagged alarm.
So a router that branches on “is the owner tag present” takes the wrong branch, silently
“The tags couldn't be retrieved when the notification was sent. CloudWatch still delivers the notification or event,
with no tags.”
Read the status field, and define the fallback. Absence of a tag is not evidence the resource is untagged.
Two pieces of design worth copying
A condition key built for exactly this toggle: cloudwatch:AlarmTagsPropagationEnabled — so you can allow alarm
creation while withholding the ability to turn propagation on.
And two shapes for two consumers: a list of objects for SNS and Lambda, key-value pairs for EventBridge
“to make event pattern filtering easier” — which also makes editing a tag a routing change.
Before you enable it
List the distinct tag keys and values on the alarms in scope. Decide which you would be happy to see in an email.
Then use an include list. It is the only mode that is closed by default for the tags nobody has written yet.
aws:-prefixed keys are “never propagated”, lists hold 1 to 50 keys, and the payload is a live read at state-change time.
